title: SYNDACTYLY, TYPE III
alt_titles: SYNDACTYLY OF FINGERS IV AND V

intro.text: This entry describes type III syndactyly (SDTY3). Isolated type III syndactyly has been suggested to map to the same region of chromosome 6q as oculodentodigital dysplasia, which is caused by mutation in the GJA1 gene and of which type III syndactyly is a feature.

checks.evidence_quote: Analysis of a large family with type III syndactyly, but atypical facial features, further suggested that isolated type III syndactyly is also located in this same region of the genome.
checks.explanation: The abstract says isolated type III syndactyly is suggested to lie in the same chromosome 6q region as the ODD locus.

checks.claim: Oculodentodigital dysplasia is caused by mutation in the GJA1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We found mutations in the GJA1 gene in all 17 families with oculodentodigital dysplasia that we screened.
checks.explanation: The title and abstract state that GJA1 mutations cause ODDD.

checks.claim: Type III syndactyly is a feature of oculodentodigital dysplasia.
checks.evidence_quote: Type III syndactyly, which occurs as part of ODD, has also been reported to occur as an isolated entity.
checks.explanation: The abstract says type III syndactyly occurs as part of ODD. Oculodentodigital syndrome (the paper's term) and oculodentodigital dysplasia are the same disorder.

paragraphs.text: Type III syndactyly is a hand malformation in which the ring and little fingers are joined. It shows autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expression (McKiernan and McCann, 1993), and brachymesophalangy of the fifth finger is a frequent association (De Smet et al., 1994). Type III syndactyly also occurs as part of oculodentodigital dysplasia, and the relationship between the isolated and syndromic forms has been debated (Brueton et al., 1990; Gladwin et al., 1997).

checks.explanation: The paper describes syndactyly joining the ring and small (little) fingers. The draft's term 'type III syndactyly' is standard naming for this condition, though the abstract doesn't use it.

checks.explanation: The abstract discusses the relationship, and the title frames it as an open question (separate entities or spectrum). This is consistent with saying the relationship has been debated.

paragraphs.text: Opjordsmoen and Nyberg-Hansen (1980) reported a family from northern Norway with a hereditary neurologic disorder consisting of spastic paraplegia associated with neurogenic bladder disturbances and syndactylia. Nine of 22 members in 3 generations had these features. The bladder disturbance, an incomplete supranuclear bladder paresis (uninhibited neurogenic bladder), was the main complaint and occurred at an early stage of the disease. The authors considered that the family probably represented an unusual form of hereditary spastic paraplegia with autosomal dominant inheritance.

paragraphs.text: Schrander-Stumpel et al. (1993) reported a newborn boy with complete cutaneous syndactyly of fingers 3 to 5 of the left hand and fingers 4 and 5 of the right hand. His mother and maternal grandmother were born with the same hand malformation. The mother had a thin nose and small teeth, and the grandmother had had very small teeth with enamel hypoplasia; eyes were normal in both. The authors considered that the family provided evidence of variable expression in oculodentodigital dysplasia.

paragraphs.text: In a genomewide search, Gladwin et al. paragraphs.text: Type III syndactyly occurs as part of oculodentodigital dysplasia (ODD) and also as an isolated entity (Gladwin et al., 1997). Brueton et al. (1990) questioned whether the 2 are separate genetic entities or a disease spectrum, and Schrander-Stumpel et al. (1993) regarded a family with type III syndactyly and subtle dental and facial findings as evidence of a clinical spectrum with ODD. Paznekas et al. (2003) identified mutations in the GJA1 gene, located at chromosome 6q22-q23, in all 17 families with ODD that they screened (16 different missense mutations and 1 codon duplication); syndactyly type III occurs in some cases of ODD.

checks.claim: Type III syndactyly occurs both as part of oculodentodigital dysplasia (ODD) and as an isolated entity.
checks.evidence_quote: Type III syndactyly, which occurs as part of ODD, has also been reported to occur as an isolated entity.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.claim: Brueton et al. (1990) questioned whether type III syndactyly and oculodentodigital dysplasia are separate genetic entities or a disease spectrum.
checks.evidence_quote: Oculodentodigital dysplasia and type III syndactyly: separate genetic entities or disease spectrum?
checks.explanation: The title poses this exact question.

checks.claim: Schrander-Stumpel et al. (1993) regarded a family with type III syndactyly and subtle dental and facial findings as evidence of a clinical spectrum with oculodentodigital dysplasia.
checks.evidence_quote: The present family provides evidence of the variable expression in oculodentodigital dysplasia.
checks.explanation: The title, 'Type III syndactyly and oculodentodigital dysplasia: a clinical spectrum,' frames the family as a clinical spectrum. The facial and dental findings (thin nose, small teeth, enamel hypoplasia) were mild and the eyes were normal. 'Subtle' is a fair description of this, although the abstract does not use that word.

checks.evidence_quote: We found mutations in the GJA1 gene in all 17 families with oculodentodigital dysplasia that we screened.
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.evidence_quote: The human connexin 43 gene, or GJA1, is located at human chromosome 6q22-q23

checks.evidence_quote: Sixteen different missense mutations and one codon duplication were detected.
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Syndactyly type III occurs in some cases of oculodentodigital dysplasia.
checks.evidence_quote: Syndactyly type III and conductive deafness can occur in some cases

agent.process_note: I opened all 9 files. Two have only a title (Johnston and Kirby 1955; Richardson et al. 2004), and the other 7 have only an abstract. None of them reports a mutation in a causal gene in families with isolated type III syndactyly. Gladwin et al. (1997) only suggested mapping to 6q, and Paznekas et al. (2003) found GJA1 mutations in oculodentodigital dysplasia (ODD) families. So I did not use the number-sign intro, and I left relationships and allelic variants empty. The Opjordsmoen family (spastic paraplegia with syndactylia) is included as reported; its abstract does not say which type of syndactyly.
